title: Project+ Study Lab
subtitle: CompTIA Project+ PK0-005 practice bank (322 questions)
note: Original practice questions written for beginners. Not affiliated with CompTIA. Check the official PK0-005 objectives before you book.

learn.idea: A project is temporary work that makes something unique. How you run it depends on the methodology: plan everything up front, or deliver in small pieces and adjust.
points: A project has a defined start and end. Operations repeat with no end date.
A program is a group of related projects managed together. A portfolio is every project and program the organisation funds to meet its strategy.
Waterfall runs phases in order and suits fixed requirements. Agile delivers in short cycles and suits changing requirements.
Project life cycle: discovery, initiating, planning, executing, monitoring and controlling, closing.
learn.memory: Projects end. Operations repeat. Programs group projects. Portfolios group everything.

cards.back: A project is temporary and unique. Operations are ongoing and repetitive.
Related projects managed together to get benefits they could not get alone.
All projects and programs an organisation chooses to fund, aligned to its strategy.
Clear, fixed requirements that are unlikely to change.
Work in progress (WIP), so work flows without overload.
Sets project standards, templates and governance across the organisation.

questions.q: Which statement best describes a project?
options: Temporary work with a defined start and end that creates a unique result
Ongoing work that keeps the business running day to day
A group of related programs managed for strategic benefit
A repeatable process with no planned end date
questions.explain: Projects are temporary and produce something unique. Ongoing, repeating work is operations.

questions.q: Which of these is operations work rather than a project?
options: Moving the company email system to the cloud
Building a new customer web portal
Installing a new data centre cooling system
questions.explain: Monthly payroll repeats with no end date, so it is operations. The others have a set end and a unique result.

questions.q: Three related projects (new CRM, data migration and staff training) are managed together so the business gets the full benefit. What is this?
questions.explain: A program groups related projects so their combined benefits can be managed.

questions.q: Which term describes all the projects and programs an organisation funds, chosen to support its strategy, even if they are not related?
questions.explain: A portfolio is the full collection of work the organisation invests in, picked to match strategy.

questions.q: A team must install network cabling to a building plan that has been signed off and cannot change. Which methodology fits best?
questions.explain: Fixed, well-understood requirements suit Waterfall's plan-first, phase-by-phase approach.

questions.q: A client wants a mobile app but expects requirements to change as users try early versions. Which approach fits best?
questions.explain: Agile delivers in short cycles and expects requirements to change based on feedback.

questions.q: A project uses a Waterfall plan for the hardware rollout and Scrum sprints for the software built on top. What is this called?
questions.explain: Hybrid mixes predictive and Agile methods within one project.

questions.q: Which project method, developed for UK government work, uses defined stages, a continued business justification and management by exception?
questions.explain: PRINCE2 is process-based, controls work in stages and checks the business case all the way through.

questions.q: A service desk team pulls tickets onto a board as capacity frees up, with a limit of three items in the In Progress column. Which framework is this?
questions.explain: Kanban visualises work on a board, limits work in progress and has no fixed sprints.

questions.q: Put the phases of the software development life cycle (SDLC) in order.
questions.explain: Requirements drive design, design drives the build, the build is tested, then deployed and maintained.

questions.q: Which approach brings development and operations teams together and relies on automation such as continuous integration and continuous delivery?
questions.explain: DevOps joins dev and ops, using automated build, test and release pipelines.

questions.q: A project can end because its objectives were met, or because it was terminated when it was no longer needed or could not succeed.
questions.explain: Both are valid endings. A cancelled project still goes through closing.

questions.q: Which methodology focuses mainly on removing waste and anything that does not add value for the customer?
questions.explain: Lean comes from manufacturing and targets waste, such as waiting, rework and extra steps.

questions.q: Which group sets project standards, templates and governance across an organisation?
options: Steering committee for one project only
questions.explain: The PMO standardises how projects are run and often supports or audits them.

questions.q: Match each methodology to its description.
pairs: Sequential phases, each finished before the next
Fixed-length sprints with set roles and events
Mix of predictive and Agile methods
questions.explain: Know what makes each one different, since the exam often asks you to pick one for a scenario.

questions.q: Put the CompTIA Project+ project life cycle phases in order.
questions.explain: Monitoring and controlling runs alongside executing. The rest happen in this order.

learn.idea: Agile delivers working pieces in short, fixed cycles and uses feedback to decide what comes next. Scrum is the most common Agile framework.
points: Product owner owns and orders the backlog. Scrum master removes blockers and coaches. The developers build the increment.
Events: sprint planning, daily stand-up, sprint review (demo) and sprint retrospective (process).
Velocity is the story points finished per sprint. Use the average to forecast.
User story format: As a role, I want a goal, so that a benefit.
learn.memory: Review shows the product. Retro improves the process.

cards.back: The product owner.

cards.front: What does the scrum master do?
cards.back: Coaches the team, protects the sprint and removes blockers.
Review demos the work to stakeholders. Retro looks at how the team worked.
Story points completed in one sprint, used to forecast.
A team estimating game that uses cards to agree on relative story points.
Minimum viable product: the smallest version that delivers value and gets feedback.

questions.q: In Scrum, who is responsible for ordering and prioritising the product backlog?
questions.explain: The product owner decides what is most valuable and orders the backlog.

questions.q: A Scrum team is blocked waiting for firewall access from another department. Whose job is it to help remove that blocker?
questions.explain: The scrum master serves the team by removing impediments.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of the daily stand-up?
options: A short daily sync on progress, plans and blockers
A full status report to the sponsor
A demo of finished work to stakeholders
A review of how the team can improve its process
questions.explain: The stand-up is about 15 minutes and keeps the team in sync. It is not a status meeting for managers.

questions.q: At the end of a sprint, the team discusses what went well and what to change about how they work. Which event is this?
questions.explain: The retrospective looks at the process. The review looks at the product.

questions.q: At the end of a sprint, the team shows the working increment to stakeholders and collects feedback. Which event is this?
questions.explain: The sprint review demos what was built so the backlog can be adjusted.

questions.q: During which event does the team choose backlog items for the coming sprint and plan how to deliver them?
questions.explain: Sprint planning sets the sprint goal and pulls items from the product backlog into the sprint backlog.

questions.q: Which is a correctly written user story?
options: As a help desk agent, I want to search tickets by user, so that I can find past issues fast
Add a search box to the ticket screen
Ticket search must be done by Friday
questions.explain: A user story names the role, the goal and the benefit.

questions.q: What does a team's velocity measure?
options: The amount of work, usually in story points, completed per sprint
The number of hours each person works per day
questions.explain: Velocity is completed work per sprint and is used to forecast future sprints.

questions.q: A team's average velocity is 27 story points per sprint. 108 points remain in the backlog. How many more sprints should it take?
questions.explain: 108 / 27 = 4 sprints.

questions.q: Which chart shows the work remaining in a sprint falling toward zero over time?
questions.explain: A burndown chart plots remaining work against time. A burnup chart shows work completed.

questions.q: The team agrees an item is not finished until it is coded, peer reviewed, tested and documented. What is this agreement called?
options: Acceptance criteria for one story only
questions.explain: The definition of done is a shared checklist that applies to every backlog item.

questions.q: What is the usual length of a Scrum sprint?
options: One to four weeks, kept the same each sprint
questions.explain: Sprints are timeboxed, usually one to four weeks, and the length stays fixed.

questions.q: The product owner and team meet mid-sprint to split large items, add detail and estimate upcoming stories. What is this?
questions.explain: Refinement keeps the top of the backlog ready for the next sprint planning.

questions.q: A large piece of work, such as 'online payments', is too big for one sprint and will be split into many stories. What is it called?
questions.explain: An epic is a big body of work broken down into user stories.

questions.q: In Scrum, any stakeholder can add new work to the current sprint at any time without discussion.
questions.explain: New requests go to the product backlog through the product owner. The sprint scope is protected once it starts.

questions.q: Match each Scrum event to its purpose.
pairs: Choose and plan the sprint's work
Demo the increment and get feedback
questions.explain: Each event has one clear job. Mixing them up is a common exam trap.

questions.q: Which value is part of the Agile Manifesto?
options: Following a plan over responding to change
Processes and tools over individuals and interactions
questions.explain: The manifesto values working software, people, collaboration and responding to change. The other options reverse it.

questions.q: A startup wants to release the smallest version of its app that delivers value so it can learn from real users. What is this called?
questions.explain: An MVP gets early feedback with the least effort.

learn.idea: Changes to an approved plan go through a formal process so their effect on scope, time, cost and risk is understood before anyone says yes.
points: Log the request, assess the impact, get a decision, then update the plan and tell people.
The change control board (CCB) approves or rejects changes. The PM does not approve them alone unless the plan allows it.
Scope creep is uncontrolled growth in scope. Gold plating is adding extras nobody asked for.
Scope, time and cost are linked. Change one and the others usually move.
learn.memory: Log, assess, decide, update, tell.

cards.front: First step for a change request?
cards.back: Log and document it.
The change control board (CCB), or whoever the change plan names.
Uncontrolled additions to scope without approval.
Adding features the customer did not ask for. Avoid it.

cards.front: What does an impact assessment cover?
cards.back: Effect on scope, schedule, cost, quality, resources and risk.
Scope, time and cost. Changing one affects the others.

questions.q: A stakeholder emails the project manager asking for a new report to be added. What should the PM do first?
options: Record it as a formal change request
Tell the developers to start on it
Reject it because scope is fixed
questions.explain: Every change starts by being documented, so it can be assessed and decided properly.

questions.q: Put the change control steps in order.
steps: Log and document the change request
Assess the impact on scope, schedule, cost and risk
Submit it to the change control board for a decision
Update the plan and baselines if approved
questions.explain: A change is never built before it is assessed and approved.

questions.q: What is the main role of the change control board?
options: Review change requests and approve or reject them
Manage the daily work of the team
questions.explain: The CCB is the decision-making group for changes to the baseline.

questions.q: Over several months, small features were added at users' request without approval, and the project is now late. What happened?
questions.explain: Scope creep is scope growing through unapproved changes.

questions.q: A department head asks a developer directly to add a feature 'since it's small'. What should the developer and PM do?
options: Send the request through the change control process
Add it quietly since it is small
Add it and tell the PM later
questions.explain: Even small changes can affect the schedule, testing and risk, so they go through change control.

questions.q: Which areas should an impact assessment look at for a change request?
options: Scope, schedule, cost, quality, resources and risk
questions.explain: A change can ripple across every constraint, so all of them are checked.

questions.q: The CCB approves a change. What should the project manager do next?
options: Update the baselines and project documents, then communicate the change
Close the change request without updating anything
Ask the CCB to approve it a second time
questions.explain: The plan must match the approved change, and the team and stakeholders must know about it.

questions.q: The CCB rejects a change request. What should happen?
options: Record the decision and reason in the change log and tell the requester
Build it anyway if the requester is senior
Delete the request from the log
Send it straight to the developers for a second opinion
questions.explain: Rejected requests stay in the change log with the reason, and the requester is told.

questions.q: Which is a product change rather than a project change?
options: Adding a new export button to the application being built
Moving the go-live date by two weeks
questions.explain: A product change alters what is being delivered. A project change alters how the project runs, such as dates, budget or people.

questions.q: On a Scrum project, how is a new feature request normally handled?
options: It is added to the product backlog and prioritised by the product owner
It goes straight into the current sprint
It needs a new project charter
It is rejected until the project ends
questions.explain: Agile expects change. New requests join the backlog and compete for priority.

questions.q: Why should project documents use version control?
options: So everyone works from the current approved version and changes can be traced
So documents can never be changed
questions.explain: Version control shows what changed, when and by whom, and stops people working from old copies.

questions.q: Gold plating, where the team adds extra features the customer did not ask for, is good practice because it raises customer satisfaction.
questions.explain: Gold plating adds unapproved scope, cost and risk. Deliver what was agreed.

questions.q: The sponsor cuts the schedule by a month but keeps the same scope. Under the triple constraint, what is most likely?
options: Cost rises or quality is at risk
questions.explain: Scope, time and cost are linked. Less time with the same scope usually means more cost or lower quality.

questions.q: Which details belong in a change log?
options: Request ID, description, requester, date, impact, status and decision
questions.explain: The change log tracks every request from start to decision, including rejected ones.

learn.idea: Break the work down, put tasks in order, estimate them, and find the longest path. That path, the critical path, sets the shortest possible project length.
points: The WBS breaks scope into deliverables. The lowest level is the work package.
Finish-to-start is the most common dependency: B starts after A finishes.
The critical path is the longest path through the network and has zero float.
Crashing adds resources (more cost). Fast tracking overlaps tasks (more risk).
learn.memory: Crash costs cash. Fast track takes a risk.

cards.front: What is the lowest level of a WBS?
cards.back: The work package.
The longest path through the schedule. Any delay on it delays the project.
How long a task can slip without delaying the project.
Crashing adds resources and cost. Fast tracking overlaps tasks and adds risk.
(Optimistic + 4 x Most likely + Pessimistic) / 6
A key point in the schedule with zero duration.

questions.q: Which document breaks the total project scope down into smaller deliverables and work packages?
questions.explain: The WBS is a hierarchy of deliverables. It shows what, not when.

questions.q: What is the lowest level of a work breakdown structure called?
questions.explain: Work packages are small enough to estimate, assign and track.

questions.q: Which document explains each WBS element, including its description, owner, acceptance criteria and estimates?
questions.explain: The WBS dictionary gives the details behind each box on the WBS.

questions.q: Server racking must finish before cabling can start. Which dependency is this?
questions.explain: Finish-to-start means the successor starts only after the predecessor finishes. It is the most common type.

questions.q: Testing can begin as soon as development begins, and they then run side by side. Which dependency is this?
questions.explain: Start-to-start means the second task can start once the first has started.

questions.q: A new concrete floor must cure for five days before equipment is installed on it. What are those five days in the schedule?
questions.explain: Lag is a forced wait between tasks. Lead lets a task start early.

questions.q: The vendor must deliver the firewall before the team can configure it, and the vendor is outside the project's control. Which kind of dependency is this?
questions.explain: An external dependency relies on someone outside the project, such as a vendor or another team.

questions.q: What is the critical path?
options: The longest path through the network, which sets the shortest possible project duration
The path with the most expensive tasks
The shortest path through the network
The list of tasks with the most risk
questions.explain: Any delay on the critical path delays the whole project, because those tasks have no float.

questions.q: Task A takes 3 days. B (5 days) and C (2 days) both follow A. D (4 days) follows both B and C. How many days long is the project?
questions.explain: Paths: A-B-D = 3 + 5 + 4 = 12. A-C-D = 3 + 2 + 4 = 9. The longest path is 12 days.

questions.q: Using the same network (A 3, B 5, C 2, D 4; B and C follow A; D follows B and C), how many days of float does task C have?
questions.explain: A-C-D is 9 days and the critical path is 12. 12 minus 9 gives C 3 days of float.

questions.q: To finish early, the PM adds two extra engineers to tasks on the critical path. Which technique is this?
questions.explain: Crashing adds resources to shorten the schedule and usually increases cost.

questions.q: To save time, the PM lets user training start before testing is fully complete. Which technique is this?
questions.explain: Fast tracking overlaps tasks that would normally run in sequence. It increases risk and possible rework.

questions.q: 'Go-live approved' appears in the schedule with zero duration. What is it?
questions.explain: Milestones mark key points or decisions and take no time themselves.

questions.q: Using a three-point PERT estimate, a task has optimistic 4 days, most likely 6 days and pessimistic 14 days. What is the estimate in days?
One engineer is booked for 70 hours in a single week. The PM moves some tasks to later weeks so the engineer is not overloaded. What is this?
questions.explain: Resource leveling adjusts the schedule to fit available people and can push the end date out.

questions.q: What is the schedule baseline?
options: The approved version of the schedule used to measure progress
The first draft written by the PM
The schedule of the previous project
questions.explain: Actual progress is compared with the baseline. Changing it needs approved change control.

questions.q: The PM estimates a firewall upgrade will take 10 days because a very similar upgrade last year took 10 days. Which estimating technique is this?
questions.explain: Analogous estimating uses a similar past project. Parametric uses a rate, such as hours per unit.

questions.q: Put the steps of building a schedule in order.
steps: Define the activities from the WBS
Develop the schedule and find the critical path
Get the schedule approved as the baseline
questions.explain: You cannot sequence tasks you have not defined, or find a critical path without durations.

learn.idea: Every project needs clear roles. Knowing who funds, who decides, who does the work and who just needs updates prevents most people problems.
points: The sponsor funds the project, approves the charter and is the top escalation point.
The PM leads the project day to day. A coordinator supports with admin and has less authority.
RACI: Responsible does it, Accountable owns it (only one), Consulted gives input, Informed is told.
Team stages: forming, storming, norming, performing, adjourning.
learn.memory: Only one A in RACI. Form, storm, norm, perform, adjourn.

cards.front: Who funds and champions the project?
cards.back: The project sponsor.
Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed.
Exactly one.
Forming, storming, norming, performing, adjourning.
Collaborating (problem solving), for a win-win.
A projectized organisation. Least is functional.

questions.q: Who provides funding for the project, approves the charter and acts as the main escalation point?
questions.explain: The sponsor champions the project and has the authority and money behind it.

questions.q: Who is responsible for leading the project team and making sure the project meets its objectives day to day?
questions.explain: The project manager plans, leads and controls the work.

questions.q: Which role supports the PM by tracking schedules, updating documents and arranging meetings, but has limited decision authority?
questions.explain: A coordinator helps with administration and communication.

questions.q: Which best defines a stakeholder?
options: Anyone who affects or is affected by the project
Only the people who fund the project
questions.explain: Stakeholders include sponsors, users, team members, vendors and anyone else with an interest.

questions.q: The team needs someone with deep knowledge of the payroll system to explain how it works. What is that person called?
questions.explain: SMEs bring specialist knowledge to the team.

questions.q: Put Tuckman's stages of team development in order.
questions.explain: Teams start polite, then clash, then agree on norms, then work well, then disband.

questions.q: A new team argues about who decides what and how work should be done. Which stage is the team in?
questions.explain: Storming is the conflict stage as people work out roles and approaches.

questions.q: In a RACI matrix, how many people should be Accountable for a single task?
questions.explain: One person owns the result. Several people can be Responsible.

questions.q: A developer reports to a functional manager but also works for a PM on a project, and both give direction. Which structure is this?
questions.explain: In a matrix structure people have two bosses, which can cause resource conflicts.

questions.q: In which organisational structure does the project manager have the most authority over the team and budget?
questions.explain: In a projectized structure teams are organised around projects and report to the PM.

questions.q: In which structure does the project manager usually have the least authority, often acting as a coordinator?
questions.explain: In a functional organisation department managers control people and budgets.

questions.q: Two engineers disagree on a design. The PM gets them to talk through each concern and agree on a solution that meets both needs. Which conflict approach is this?
questions.explain: Collaborating looks for a win-win and gives the most lasting result.

questions.q: Match each conflict approach to its description.
pairs: Play up agreement and play down differences
Withdraw from the conflict for now
questions.explain: Collaborating is usually best. Forcing suits emergencies. Avoiding can buy time but rarely fixes anything.

questions.q: A functional manager pulls a shared DBA off the project for two weeks to work on operations. What should the PM do first?
options: Discuss and negotiate with the functional manager, and assess the schedule impact
Hire a new DBA without telling anyone
Remove the DBA's tasks from scope
questions.explain: In a matrix, shared resources are negotiated. Assess the impact and escalate to the sponsor if you cannot agree.

learn.idea: A risk might happen. An issue is happening now. Find risks early, judge them, plan a response, and keep watching them.
points: Negative risk responses: avoid, transfer, mitigate, accept.
Positive risk responses: exploit, enhance, share, accept.
Qualitative analysis ranks risks with a probability and impact matrix. Quantitative puts numbers on them, such as EMV.
EMV = probability x impact.
learn.memory: Threats: Avoid, Transfer, Mitigate, Accept. Opportunities: Exploit, Enhance, Share, Accept.

cards.back: A risk may happen. An issue has happened.
Buying insurance or outsourcing to a vendor on a fixed price.
Reduce the probability or impact of a risk.
Probability x impact.
A warning sign that a risk is about to happen.
An unplanned response to a problem that has already happened.

questions.q: What is the difference between a risk and an issue?
options: A risk is uncertain and in the future. An issue has already happened.
A risk is always negative. An issue is always positive.
A risk affects cost only. An issue affects schedule only.
questions.explain: Risks go in the risk register. When one happens, it becomes an issue in the issue log.

questions.q: Where are identified risks, their ratings, owners and planned responses recorded?
questions.explain: The risk register is the main tool for tracking risks.

questions.q: A risky new database version could delay the project, so the team decides to use the proven current version instead. Which response is this?
questions.explain: Avoiding changes the plan so the risk no longer applies.

questions.q: The company buys insurance against hardware damage during shipping. Which risk response is this?
questions.explain: Transfer shifts the impact to a third party, such as an insurer or vendor.

questions.q: The team adds extra testing to reduce the chance that a data migration will fail. Which risk response is this?
questions.explain: Mitigation lowers the probability or impact of a risk.

questions.q: A minor risk would cost more to address than its impact, so the team sets aside a small contingency and moves on. Which response is this?
questions.explain: Acceptance can be active (with a contingency reserve) or passive (deal with it if it happens).

questions.q: A vendor offers a discount if the order is placed this month. The PM makes sure the order goes in on time to secure it. Which positive risk response is this?
questions.explain: Exploit makes sure an opportunity definitely happens.

questions.q: Match each positive risk response to its description.
pairs: Partner with someone better able to capture it
Take the benefit if it comes, with no action
questions.explain: These mirror the negative responses: exploit is the opposite of avoid, share of transfer, enhance of mitigate.

questions.q: The team rates each risk as high, medium or low for probability and impact, and plots them on a grid. What is this?
questions.explain: Qualitative analysis uses ratings and a probability and impact matrix to rank risks quickly.

questions.q: Which is a quantitative risk analysis technique?
questions.explain: Quantitative analysis puts numbers on risk, such as EMV or Monte Carlo simulation.

questions.q: A risk has a 30% probability and would cost $20,000 if it happens. What is its expected monetary value in dollars?
Who should watch a specific risk and carry out its response if it happens?
options: The risk owner named in the risk register
Nobody until it becomes an issue
questions.explain: Each risk gets an owner who tracks it and acts on the response plan.

questions.q: A key vendor stops replying to emails, a warning sign that a delivery delay is coming. What is this warning sign called?
questions.explain: Triggers show that a risk is about to happen, so the response can start.

questions.q: Which reserve is set aside for known risks that were identified and analysed?
questions.explain: Contingency covers known risks. Management reserve covers unknown risks and is controlled by management.

questions.q: Put the risk management steps in order.
questions.explain: You must find a risk before you can rate it, plan for it, and then watch it.

questions.q: A server fails with no plan in place for it, so the team moves the application to a spare server to keep working. What is this?
questions.explain: A workaround is an unplanned fix for a problem that has already happened.

learn.idea: Most project problems are communication problems. Plan who needs what information, how often and in what form.
points: Communication channels = n x (n - 1) / 2, where n is the number of people.
The communication plan covers who, what, when, how and how often.
Email and chat are asynchronous. Meetings and calls are synchronous.
Manage high-power, high-interest stakeholders closely. Keep high-power, low-interest ones satisfied.
learn.memory: Channels: n times n minus one, halved.

cards.front: What goes in a communication plan?
cards.back: Who, what, when, how, how often and who sends it.
A meeting or phone call.
Email, chat or a shared document.
Keep satisfied.

cards.front: Best way to give bad news to a sponsor?
cards.back: Directly and early, in person or a call, then follow up in writing.

questions.q: A project has 10 people who need to communicate. How many communication channels are there?
A team grows from 6 to 9 people. How many communication channels are added?
questions.explain: Before: 6 x 5 / 2 = 15. After: 9 x 8 / 2 = 36. 36 minus 15 = 21.

questions.q: Which document says who needs project information, what they need, how often and by what method?
questions.explain: The communication plan sets how information flows to each stakeholder.

questions.q: Which communication method is asynchronous?
questions.explain: With asynchronous methods people read and reply when they can, not at the same time.

questions.q: A major milestone will be missed. How should the PM tell the sponsor?
options: Directly and early, in a meeting or call, then follow up in writing
In a group email to the whole company
Wait until the next monthly report
Ask a team member to mention it
questions.explain: Bad news should reach the sponsor quickly and directly, with a written record afterwards.

questions.q: On a power and interest grid, how should a stakeholder with high power but low interest be managed?
questions.explain: High power and high interest: manage closely. High power and low interest: keep satisfied.

questions.q: Which form of communication should be used for a change to a vendor contract?
questions.explain: Contracts and legal matters need formal, written, recorded communication.

questions.q: The team is spread across Jamaica, the UK and India. What helps communication most?
options: Rotate meeting times and use shared async tools
Hold every meeting at 9 AM Jamaica time
Send updates only at the end of the project
questions.explain: Rotating times shares the burden, and async tools let people catch up in their own working hours.

questions.q: What do senior executives usually want from a project status report?
options: A short summary, such as a dashboard of key measures and red flags
Every task detail from the schedule
questions.explain: Tailor the message to the audience. Executives want the big picture and decisions needed.

questions.q: A key stakeholder ignores repeated requests for sign-off and it is now delaying the project. What should the PM do?
options: Follow the escalation path in the communication plan, such as raising it to the sponsor
Remove them from the stakeholder register
questions.explain: When normal communication fails, escalate through the agreed path.

learn.idea: Before a project starts, someone has to show it is worth doing. The business case compares costs, benefits and options so leaders can pick the best investment.
points: The business case explains why the project is needed, the options, costs, benefits and risks.
ROI = (gain minus cost) / cost. Payback period = cost / yearly savings.
Pick the higher NPV or IRR. Pick the shorter payback.
Sunk costs are already spent and should not drive the decision.
learn.memory: Higher NPV, higher IRR, shorter payback.

cards.back: The justification for a project: need, options, costs, benefits and risks.
(Gain minus cost) / cost, as a percentage.
Cost divided by yearly savings: how long until the money comes back.
Choose the project with the highest positive NPV.
The value of the best option you gave up.
Money already spent. It should not decide whether to continue.

questions.q: Which document explains why a project should be done, including the options, expected costs, benefits and risks?
questions.explain: The business case justifies the investment. The charter then authorises the project.

questions.q: A project costs $50,000 and returns $65,000 in benefits. What is the ROI as a percentage?
A new system costs $120,000 and saves $30,000 a year. What is the payback period in years?
Project A has an NPV of $40,000 and Project B has an NPV of $25,000. Both cost the same. Which should be chosen on NPV alone?
questions.explain: A higher positive NPV means more value in today's money.

questions.q: When comparing projects by internal rate of return (IRR), which is preferred?
questions.explain: A higher IRR means a better return on the investment.

questions.q: Before committing, the organisation checks whether the project is technically, financially and operationally possible. What is this?
questions.explain: A feasibility study tests whether the project can realistically succeed.

questions.q: The team compares how the help desk works today with how it should work, to find what is missing. What is this?
questions.explain: Gap analysis compares the current state with the desired state.

questions.q: Which activity belongs in the discovery (concept) phase?
options: Defining the business need and high-level requirements
questions.explain: Discovery works out the problem, the need and whether a project should go ahead.

questions.q: A committee ranks candidate projects by scoring each one against criteria such as strategic fit, cost and risk, with each criterion weighted. What is this?
questions.explain: A weighted scoring model compares options against agreed, weighted criteria.

questions.q: The company can fund only one project: Project A worth $100,000 or Project B worth $70,000. It picks A. What is the opportunity cost in dollars?
questions.explain: The opportunity cost is the value of the best option given up, which is B at $70,000.

questions.q: Money already spent on a failing project should be the main reason to keep funding it.
questions.explain: That is the sunk cost fallacy. Decide based on future costs and benefits only.

questions.q: Why is $10,000 today worth more than $10,000 received in five years?
options: Money today can be invested and earn a return (time value of money)
Future money is always taxed more
Banks do not accept future money
questions.explain: The time value of money is the reason NPV discounts future cash flows.

questions.q: Who typically reviews and approves the business case so the project can move into initiating?
options: The sponsor or a governance committee
questions.explain: Funding decisions sit with the sponsor or the organisation's governance group.

questions.q: A project's benefits will not appear until two years after it ends. Which measure helps compare it fairly with a project that pays back sooner?
questions.explain: NPV discounts future benefits so projects with different timing can be compared.

learn.idea: Initiating makes the project official. The sponsor signs a charter that names the PM, sets high-level goals and gives the authority to start.
points: The project charter formally authorises the project and gives the PM authority.
The sponsor signs the charter.
Assumptions are things believed to be true without proof. Constraints are limits.
The kickoff meeting aligns everyone on goals, roles and next steps.
learn.memory: No signed charter, no project.

cards.back: Formally authorises the project and gives the PM authority.
The project sponsor.
Something believed true without proof, such as 'the vendor ships on time'.
A limit, such as a fixed budget or deadline.
Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound.
Align the team and stakeholders on goals, roles and plans.

questions.q: Which document formally authorises a project and gives the project manager authority to use resources?
questions.explain: The charter is the official start of the project.

questions.q: Who normally signs the project charter?
questions.explain: The sponsor has the authority and funding, so the sponsor signs.

questions.q: Which item belongs in a project charter?
options: High-level objectives, success criteria and milestones
Detailed task durations for every work package
questions.explain: The charter is high level. Detail comes in planning.

questions.q: The team plans as if the cloud provider will give them a test environment by March, but this is not confirmed. What is this?
questions.explain: An assumption is believed true without proof. It should be logged and checked.

questions.q: The budget cannot go above $250,000 and go-live must be before the tax year ends. What are these?
questions.explain: Constraints limit the project's options.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of a project kickoff meeting?
options: Align the team and stakeholders on objectives, roles and next steps
questions.explain: Kickoff gets everyone started with the same understanding.

questions.q: Which objective is written in SMART form?
options: Move 300 mailboxes to the cloud with no data loss by 30 June
Do a good job on the migration
questions.explain: It is specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound.

questions.q: Which is a measurable success criterion?
options: Help desk calls about password resets drop by 40% within three months
questions.explain: Success criteria must be measurable so the result can be checked.

questions.q: Which document lists everyone with an interest in the project, along with their role, interest and influence?
questions.explain: The stakeholder register is started in initiating and kept up to date.

questions.q: What does a preliminary (high-level) scope statement do during initiating?
options: Gives a first outline of what the project will and will not deliver
Lists every task with its duration
Replaces the need for a detailed scope statement
questions.explain: It gives an early boundary. The detailed scope statement comes in planning.

questions.q: When are high-level risks first identified and recorded?
options: During initiating, often in the charter
Never, risks appear on their own
questions.explain: High-level risks go in the charter, then the risk register grows in planning.

questions.q: The detailed work breakdown structure is created during the initiating phase.
questions.explain: The WBS is a planning activity. Initiating stays at a high level.

questions.q: Put these early project steps in order.
questions.explain: The business case leads to the charter. Once it is signed, the PM identifies stakeholders and holds the kickoff.

questions.q: Where does the project manager's authority to run the project come from?
questions.explain: The charter names the PM and states their level of authority.

learn.idea: Planning turns the charter into a detailed, approved plan: exactly what will be built, how, when, by whom, for how much and to what quality.
points: The scope statement lists deliverables, exclusions and acceptance criteria.
Cost baseline = cost estimates + contingency reserve. Budget = cost baseline + management reserve.
Quality assurance improves the process. Quality control inspects the product.
The project management plan pulls all the subsidiary plans together.
learn.memory: QA checks the process. QC checks the product.

cards.front: What does the scope statement include?
cards.back: Deliverables, exclusions, acceptance criteria, assumptions and constraints.
Cost baseline (estimates + contingency) + management reserve.
QA prevents defects by improving the process. QC finds defects by inspecting output.
Bottom-up: estimate each work package and add them up.
About -25% to +75%. Used very early.
Plan near-term work in detail and later work in less detail.

questions.q: Which document gives a detailed description of the project's deliverables, exclusions and acceptance criteria?
questions.explain: The scope statement sets exactly what is and is not in the project.

questions.q: Why should the scope statement list exclusions (what is out of scope)?
options: To prevent misunderstandings and scope creep
questions.explain: Writing down what is not included stops people assuming it is.

questions.q: A business analyst sits with call centre staff for a day to watch how they use the current system. Which requirements technique is this?
questions.explain: Observation shows how work is really done, including steps people forget to mention.

questions.q: Which is a non-functional requirement?
options: Pages must load in under two seconds
Users can reset their own password
The system can print an invoice
questions.explain: Non-functional requirements describe how well the system works, such as speed, security or availability.

questions.q: What is the cost baseline?
options: The approved, time-phased budget used to measure cost performance
questions.explain: Actual spending is compared to the cost baseline. It excludes management reserve.

questions.q: The team estimates every work package and adds them together to get the project total. Which technique is this?
questions.explain: Bottom-up is slow but the most accurate.

questions.q: Imaging one workstation costs $150. Using parametric estimating, what is the cost to image 200 workstations, in dollars?
Work package estimates total $80,000. The contingency reserve is $8,000 and the management reserve is $12,000. What is the total project budget in dollars?
The PM sets up peer code reviews and a standard testing process so fewer defects are created. What is this?
questions.explain: QA focuses on the process, to prevent defects.

questions.q: Testers check each finished report against its specification and log any defects found. What is this?
questions.explain: QC inspects the deliverables to find defects.

questions.q: Which is a prevention cost in the cost of quality?
options: Training the team before work starts
questions.explain: Prevention costs are spent up front to avoid defects. Fixing failures is a failure cost.

questions.q: The team decides whether to build a reporting tool in-house or buy one from a vendor. What is this?
questions.explain: Make-or-buy analysis is part of procurement planning.

questions.q: Which tool shows when each team member is available, including holidays and other commitments?
questions.explain: Resource calendars stop you scheduling work for people who are away.

questions.q: Which plan describes how the finished system will be handed over to the operations and support teams?
questions.explain: The transition plan covers handover, training, documentation and support.

questions.q: Which document brings together the scope, schedule, cost, quality, risk, communication and other plans?
questions.explain: The project management plan is the master plan made up of the subsidiary plans.

questions.q: Very early in discovery, the sponsor asks for a quick estimate knowing it may be well off. What is this called?
questions.explain: A ROM estimate is fast and has a wide range, about -25% to +75%.

questions.q: Put these planning steps in order.
questions.explain: Requirements shape scope, scope is broken into the WBS, the WBS drives the schedule, and the schedule and resources drive the budget.

questions.q: The PM plans the next two months in detail and leaves later phases at a high level until more is known. What is this?
questions.explain: Rolling wave planning adds detail as the work gets closer.

learn.idea: Executing is where the plan becomes real: the team builds, the PM leads, vendors deliver and quality is managed.
points: RFI gathers information. RFQ asks for a price on a known item. RFP asks for a full proposal.
Fixed price puts the cost risk on the seller. Cost-plus puts it on the buyer.
Time and materials pays an hourly rate plus materials and suits unclear scope.
Choose vendors with weighted criteria, not price alone.
learn.memory: Info, Quote, Proposal: RFI, RFQ, RFP.

cards.back: Request for information: learn what vendors can offer.
Request for quote: price for a clearly defined item.
Request for proposal: full solution proposals for complex needs.
Mostly on the seller.
Mostly on the buyer.
Work with unclear scope or short-term staff.

questions.q: Which activity mainly happens during the executing phase?
options: Building the deliverables and managing the team
questions.explain: Executing carries out the plan and produces the deliverables.

questions.q: The PM wants to learn which vendors offer managed backup services and what they can do, before writing detailed requirements. Which document should be sent?
questions.explain: An RFI gathers general information about vendors and options.

questions.q: The team needs a price for 50 identical laptops with a known specification. Which document fits?
questions.explain: An RFQ asks for prices on clearly defined goods.

questions.q: The organisation needs vendors to design and propose a full disaster recovery solution. Which document fits?
questions.explain: An RFP asks vendors to propose how they would solve a complex need.

questions.q: Put the procurement steps in order.
steps: Send an RFI to learn the market
Issue an RFP to shortlisted vendors
questions.explain: Learn the market, ask for proposals, evaluate, choose, contract, then manage delivery.

questions.q: In a fixed-price contract, who carries most of the cost risk?
questions.explain: The price is set, so cost overruns hurt the seller.

questions.q: In a cost-plus (cost-reimbursable) contract, who carries most of the cost risk?
questions.explain: The buyer pays the seller's costs plus a fee, so overruns hurt the buyer.

questions.q: The scope is unclear, so the company hires a contractor at an hourly rate plus the cost of any parts used. Which contract type is this?
questions.explain: Time and materials suits short or unclear work.

questions.q: What is the best way to select a vendor from several proposals?
options: Score each against weighted criteria such as price, experience, support and risk
Pick the vendor the sponsor knows
questions.explain: Weighted criteria give a fair, defensible choice.

questions.q: All interested vendors attend one meeting to ask questions about the RFP and hear the same answers. What is this?
questions.explain: A bidders conference keeps the process fair, with every vendor getting the same information.

questions.q: During executing, the quality team checks whether the project is following its defined testing process. What is this?
questions.explain: Audits check that processes are followed, which is quality assurance.

questions.q: The team has hit a tough milestone. Which action best builds team morale and performance?
questions.explain: Recognition motivates the team and reinforces good work.

questions.q: What should meeting minutes include so the meeting leads to results?
options: Decisions made and action items with owners and due dates
questions.explain: Action items with owners and dates turn talk into work.

questions.q: A department manager keeps resisting the new system. What should the PM do first?
options: Meet them to understand their concerns and address them
questions.explain: Understanding the reason for resistance is the first step to gaining support.

questions.q: A test server crashes and blocks testing. Where should this be recorded, with an owner and due date?
questions.explain: Problems happening now go in the issue log and are tracked to resolution.

questions.q: Staff must learn new processes to use the new system. Which activity helps them adopt it?
options: Organisational change management, such as training and clear communication
questions.explain: Change management helps people accept and use what the project delivers.

questions.q: Contractor staff are about to start working on company systems. What should happen first?
options: They sign any required NDA and get approved access
They are given the admin password by email
They start work and paperwork follows later
They borrow a staff member's login
questions.explain: Contractors need legal agreements and proper, approved access before touching systems.

learn.idea: Monitoring compares actual progress with the plan. Earned value turns that comparison into numbers so you can see if you are over budget or behind schedule.
points: PV = planned value, EV = earned value (work done), AC = actual cost.
CV = EV - AC. SV = EV - PV. Negative is bad.
CPI = EV / AC. SPI = EV / PV. Below 1 is bad.
EAC = BAC / CPI. ETC = EAC - AC. VAC = BAC - EAC.
learn.memory: EV comes first in all four variance and index formulas.

cards.back: EV - AC. Negative means over budget.
EV - PV. Negative means behind schedule.
EV / AC. Below 1 means over budget.
EV / PV. Below 1 means behind schedule.
BAC / CPI
Corrective fixes a variance already found. Preventive stops a likely future one.

questions.q: In earned value management, what is planned value (PV)?
options: The budgeted cost of the work scheduled to be done by now
The actual money spent so far
The budgeted value of the work actually completed
questions.explain: PV is what you planned to have done by this date, in budget terms.

questions.q: What is earned value (EV)?
options: The budgeted value of the work actually completed
The work planned for this date
questions.explain: EV measures progress in budget terms.

questions.q: What is actual cost (AC)?
options: The money actually spent on the work done so far
The budget for the whole project
questions.explain: AC is what has really been paid.

questions.q: EV is $40,000 and AC is $50,000. What is the cost variance (CV) in dollars?
questions.explain: CV = EV - AC = 40,000 - 50,000 = -10,000. Negative means over budget.

questions.q: EV is $40,000 and PV is $45,000. What is the schedule variance (SV) in dollars?
questions.explain: SV = EV - PV = 40,000 - 45,000 = -5,000. Negative means behind schedule.

questions.q: EV is $40,000 and AC is $50,000. What is the cost performance index (CPI)?
EV is $45,000 and PV is $50,000. What is the schedule performance index (SPI)?
A project has a CPI of 1.2 and an SPI of 0.8. What does this mean?
options: Over budget and ahead of schedule
Under budget and ahead of schedule
questions.explain: CPI above 1 is under budget. SPI below 1 is behind schedule.

questions.q: The budget at completion (BAC) is $200,000 and the CPI is 0.8. What is the estimate at completion (EAC) in dollars?
The EAC is $250,000 and the actual cost so far is $100,000. What is the estimate to complete (ETC) in dollars?
The BAC is $200,000 and the EAC is $250,000. What is the variance at completion (VAC) in dollars?
questions.explain: VAC = BAC - EAC = 200,000 - 250,000 = -50,000. The project is expected to finish $50,000 over budget.

questions.q: A project has a BAC of $100,000 and is 40% complete. What is its earned value in dollars?
questions.explain: EV = percent complete x BAC = 0.40 x 100,000 = 40,000.

questions.q: Which is a key performance indicator (KPI) for a help desk migration project?
options: Percentage of tickets resolved within the SLA
questions.explain: A KPI is a measurable value that shows whether goals are being met.

questions.q: The project's CPI drops below the 0.9 tolerance set in the plan. What should the PM do?
options: Analyse the cause and take corrective action, escalating if needed
Hide the figure from the report
questions.explain: Crossing a set threshold triggers analysis and corrective action.

questions.q: Testers compare a finished deliverable against its acceptance criteria before it goes to the customer. Which process is this?
questions.explain: QC inspects and tests deliverables to find defects.

questions.q: Match each action to its description.
pairs: Fixes a variance that has already happened
Reduces the chance of a future variance
Formal ask to change the baseline
questions.explain: All four can come out of monitoring and controlling.

questions.q: The customer formally reviews and accepts completed deliverables. What is this process?
questions.explain: Validate scope is the customer's formal acceptance. Quality control happens before it.

questions.q: An independent team checks whether the project followed data protection rules. What is this?
questions.explain: Audits check that the project meets required standards and rules.

questions.q: On a red, amber and green (RAG) status dashboard, what does red usually mean?
options: Serious problems that need action or escalation
questions.explain: Red signals trouble, amber means at risk, and green means on track.

questions.q: Monitoring and controlling happens only at the end of the project.
questions.explain: It runs through the whole project, alongside executing, so problems are caught early.

learn.idea: Closing makes the end official: the customer accepts, the work is handed over, contracts and budgets are closed, lessons are captured and people are released.
points: Get formal sign-off that the deliverables are accepted.
Hand over to operations with documentation, training and support.
Close contracts and financial codes so nothing more is charged.
Capture lessons learned, release resources and archive records.
learn.memory: Accept, hand over, learn, release, archive.

cards.back: Get formal acceptance and sign-off.
Record what worked and what did not, so future projects benefit.
Extra support just after go-live while users settle in.

cards.front: Does a cancelled project still close?
cards.back: Yes. Document why, capture lessons and close it properly.
Confirm all deliverables received, settle invoices, close the agreement.
All through the project, not just at the end.

questions.q: What is the first thing that should happen when the project's deliverables are complete?
options: Get formal acceptance and sign-off from the customer or sponsor
questions.explain: Formal acceptance confirms the work meets the agreed criteria.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of a lessons learned session?
options: Record what went well and what to improve for future projects
questions.explain: Lessons learned help the organisation get better at projects.

questions.q: Put these closing activities in order.
steps: Obtain formal acceptance of the deliverables
Hold the lessons learned session with the team
Release resources and archive project records
questions.explain: Accept first, hand over, capture lessons while the team is still there, then release people and archive.

questions.q: What does closing a vendor contract involve?
options: Confirming all deliverables were received and settling final invoices
questions.explain: Contract closure confirms obligations are met on both sides.

questions.q: What makes a good handover to operations?
options: Documentation, training and agreed support arrangements
An email with the server password
Leaving the team to support it forever
Nothing, operations will work it out
questions.explain: Operations needs the knowledge and tools to run the solution.

questions.q: The sponsor cancels the project halfway through. What should the PM do?
options: Run a proper closure: document the reason, capture lessons learned and archive records
Stop work and leave everything as it is
Keep working until the original end date
questions.explain: Terminated projects are closed formally too, and their lessons can be valuable.

questions.q: How should project records be handled at closing?
options: Archived according to the organisation's retention policy
questions.explain: Records may be needed for audits, legal reasons or future projects.

questions.q: When releasing team members at the end of the project, what should the PM do?
options: Tell their functional managers and give feedback on their performance
Keep them on the project code indefinitely
Ask them to find new work themselves
questions.explain: Proper release helps people move on and gives managers useful feedback.

questions.q: What does a final project report usually include?
options: Performance against scope, schedule, cost and quality, plus key lessons
questions.explain: The final report summarises how the project did against its goals.

questions.q: Why should the PM celebrate and recognise the team at the end of the project?
options: It rewards effort and builds goodwill for future work
questions.explain: Recognition helps morale and makes people keen to work together again.

questions.q: After go-live, the project team gives extra support for two weeks while users settle in, before full handover to the help desk. What is this?
questions.explain: Hypercare catches early problems before normal support takes over.

questions.q: Lessons learned should be collected only at the very end of the project.
questions.explain: Capture them throughout, while details are fresh. Closing gathers them together.

questions.q: The customer refuses to sign off, saying the system 'is not what they wanted'. What should the PM refer to?
options: The acceptance criteria agreed in the scope statement
The first draft of the business case
questions.explain: Agreed acceptance criteria are the objective test of whether the deliverable is done.

questions.q: Why should the project's budget codes be closed at the end?
options: So no further costs can be charged to the project
So the team gets paid faster
questions.explain: Closing financial accounts stops stray charges and gives a final cost figure.

learn.idea: The right tool makes the plan visible. Gantt charts show time, Kanban boards show flow, ticketing systems track requests, and dashboards sum it all up.
points: Gantt charts show tasks as bars over time, with dependencies and progress.
Kanban boards show work moving through columns such as To do, In progress and Done.
Ticketing systems track tasks, requests and defects with owners and status.
Shared repositories with version control keep one source of truth for documents and code.
learn.memory: Gantt for time, Kanban for flow, dashboard for the boss.

cards.back: Tasks as bars over time, with dependencies and progress.
Work moving through stages, with WIP limits.
An at-a-glance view of key measures and status.
One current version of every document, with history.
Timesheets and invoices.
A secure, company-approved tool, not personal apps.

questions.q: Which tool shows project tasks as horizontal bars along a timeline, often with dependencies and percent complete?
questions.explain: A Gantt chart is the classic schedule view.

questions.q: A team tracks work on a board with columns for Backlog, In progress, Testing and Done. What is this tool?
questions.explain: A Kanban board makes the flow of work and any bottlenecks easy to see.

questions.q: Which feature of project scheduling software helps the PM most when tasks slip?
options: It recalculates dates and the critical path from task dependencies
questions.explain: Linked tasks let the software show the knock-on effect of a delay.

questions.q: The team needs to log bugs and requests, assign them to people and track their status. Which tool fits?
questions.explain: Ticketing systems give each item an ID, owner, priority and status history.

questions.q: Team members keep editing different copies of the requirements document. What fixes this?
options: A shared repository with version control
questions.explain: A shared repository keeps one current version and a record of changes.

questions.q: A developer has a quick question for a colleague in the same team. Which tool fits best?
questions.explain: Chat suits quick, informal questions. Decisions should still be recorded properly.

questions.q: The sponsor wants an at-a-glance view of schedule, budget and risk status. Which tool fits?
questions.explain: Dashboards summarise key measures visually, often with red, amber and green.

questions.q: The team is spread across time zones. Which tool helps most with booking meetings?
options: A shared calendar that shows each person's free time and time zone
questions.explain: Shared calendars avoid booking people outside their working hours.

questions.q: Which tool tracks changes to source code, lets developers work on branches and allows rollback?
options: A version control system such as Git
questions.explain: Version control keeps the full history of code changes.

questions.q: The PM needs input from 400 staff about how they use the current intranet. Which tool is most efficient?
questions.explain: Surveys gather answers from many people quickly.

questions.q: During a brainstorming session, the team maps out ideas and how they connect. Which tool fits?
options: A mind map or digital whiteboard
questions.explain: Mind maps and whiteboards help capture and group ideas visually.

questions.q: Which tool supplies the hours worked that feed into the project's actual cost?
questions.explain: Timesheets show real effort, which drives actual cost and future estimates.

questions.q: The team needs to share customer data files during the project. Which choice is best?
options: A secure, company-approved file sharing tool with access controls
A public link anyone can open
questions.explain: Sensitive data should stay in approved, controlled tools.

questions.q: A Gantt chart can show task durations, dependencies and progress against the timeline.
questions.explain: Most scheduling tools draw dependencies as arrows and shade bars to show progress.

questions.q: Match each tool to its main use.
questions.explain: Pick the tool that answers the question being asked.

learn.idea: Projects run on documents. Agreements set the legal terms with vendors, and logs and reports keep track of what is happening.
points: SOW describes the work and deliverables. MSA sets general terms for future work. SLA sets service levels.
NDA protects confidential information. MOU states shared intent and is usually not legally binding.
A purchase order (PO) authorises a purchase. An invoice asks for payment.
Logs: issue log (problems now), risk register (may happen), change log (requests), decision log (decisions).
learn.memory: MSA is the umbrella. SOW is the job. SLA is the promise.

cards.back: Statement of work: the work, deliverables and timeline a vendor will provide.
Master services agreement: general terms that cover future SOWs.
Service level agreement: measurable service targets such as uptime.
Non-disclosure agreement: protects confidential information.
Memorandum of understanding: shared intent, usually not legally binding.
Links each requirement to its deliverable and test.

questions.q: Which document describes the specific work, deliverables and timeline a vendor will provide?
questions.explain: The SOW defines exactly what the vendor will do.

questions.q: A company signs one agreement with a vendor that sets payment terms, liability and confidentiality for all future work, then adds separate SOWs for each job. What is the main agreement?
questions.explain: The MSA sets the general terms so each new job only needs a SOW.

questions.q: A hosting provider promises 99.9% uptime and a four-hour response to critical incidents. Which document sets these targets?
questions.explain: An SLA defines measurable service levels.

questions.q: Before sharing network diagrams with a possible vendor, what should the vendor sign?
questions.explain: An NDA legally protects confidential information.

questions.q: Two government agencies agree in writing to work together on a shared portal, but neither is legally bound yet. Which document is this?
questions.explain: An MOU records shared intent and is usually not legally binding.

questions.q: Which document from the buyer authorises a purchase and states the items, quantities and agreed prices?
questions.explain: The PO is the buyer's formal commitment to buy.

questions.q: Which document does a vendor send to request payment for delivered goods or services?
questions.explain: The invoice is checked against the PO and what was actually received.

questions.q: A new switch fails after three months. Which document says whether the vendor must replace it for free?
questions.explain: A warranty covers repair or replacement for a set period.

questions.q: Which of these is a legally binding agreement between buyer and seller?
questions.explain: Contracts are enforceable. MOUs and RFIs are not.

questions.q: Match each log to what it records.
pairs: Key decisions, who made them and why
questions.explain: Each log has one job. Exam questions often swap them to test you.

questions.q: Which document shows who is Responsible, Accountable, Consulted and Informed for each deliverable?
questions.explain: The RACI chart makes ownership clear.

questions.q: What should be sent to attendees before a meeting so they can prepare?
options: An agenda with topics, timings and the meeting goal
questions.explain: Agendas keep meetings focused. Minutes come afterwards.

questions.q: What does a typical weekly status report include?
options: Progress since last report, next steps, key issues and risks
questions.explain: Status reports summarise where the project stands and what needs attention.

questions.q: Which document lists every task with its start and finish dates, dependencies and assigned resources?
questions.explain: The schedule shows when work happens and who does it.

questions.q: Which document links each requirement to the deliverable that meets it and the test that proves it?
questions.explain: The traceability matrix makes sure nothing is missed or built without a requirement.

questions.q: Where are lessons captured during the project so they are not forgotten by the end?
questions.explain: A running register stops lessons being lost before closing.

questions.q: How long should project records be kept after closing?
options: As long as the organisation's records retention policy requires
Until the PM leaves the company
questions.explain: Retention periods come from policy, law and contracts.

questions.q: The steering committee chooses Vendor B over Vendor A. Where should the choice, the reason and who made it be recorded?
questions.explain: The decision log stops the same decision being reopened and shows who agreed it.

questions.q: Which document describes how the solution will be tested, including scope, approach, environments and pass criteria?
questions.explain: The test plan guides testing and shows what counts as a pass.

questions.q: An SLA promises 99.9% uptime over a 30-day month. How many minutes of downtime are allowed?
questions.explain: 30 x 24 x 60 = 43,200 minutes. 0.1% of that is 43.2 minutes.

questions.q: A vendor misses the SLA uptime target. What does the SLA usually give the customer?
options: Service credits or penalties as set out in the agreement
questions.explain: SLAs often include service credits when targets are missed.

questions.q: For a server room build, which document lists every hardware part and its quantity?
questions.explain: A BOM is the parts list used for ordering and checking deliveries.

questions.q: Put these vendor documents in the order they are usually used.
steps: NDA signed so information can be shared
Proposal selected and contract (MSA and SOW) signed
questions.explain: Protect information, ask for proposals, contract the winner, authorise the purchase, then pay.

questions.q: A memorandum of understanding is normally a legally binding contract that can be enforced in court.
questions.explain: An MOU usually shows shared intent only. A contract is what binds the parties.

learn.idea: Charts turn data into decisions. Each one answers a different question: what causes most problems, what caused this one, is the process stable, how are we progressing.
points: Pareto: biggest causes first. About 80% of problems come from 20% of causes.
Fishbone (Ishikawa): possible causes of one problem, grouped by category.
Control chart: is a process stable within its limits over time?
Scatter diagram: is there a relationship between two variables?
learn.memory: Pareto picks the problem. Fishbone finds the cause.

cards.back: Bars in descending order with a cumulative line, to find the vital few causes.
Cause and effect diagram that groups possible causes of one problem.
Seven points in a row on one side of the mean means investigate.
Shows how often values fall into ranges (frequency).
Shows whether two variables are related.
Shows work completed rising toward total scope.

questions.q: Which chart shows causes in descending order of frequency, with a cumulative percentage line, to find the vital few?
questions.explain: Pareto charts help you fix the biggest causes first.

questions.q: The team wants to brainstorm all possible causes of slow network performance, grouped into people, process, equipment and environment. Which tool fits?
questions.explain: The fishbone diagram organises possible causes of one effect.

questions.q: Which chart shows how often values fall into ranges, such as how many tickets took 0 to 1 hours, 1 to 2 hours and so on?
questions.explain: A histogram shows the distribution of data.

questions.q: The PM wants to know whether more overtime is linked to more defects. Which chart fits?
questions.explain: A scatter diagram plots two variables to show any relationship.

questions.q: Which chart shows whether a process stays within upper and lower limits over time?
questions.explain: Control charts show whether a process is stable or needs attention.

questions.q: On a control chart, seven data points in a row fall above the mean but inside the control limits. What does this mean?
options: The process may be out of control and should be investigated
Nothing, all points are inside the limits
questions.explain: The rule of seven flags a pattern that is unlikely to be random.

questions.q: Which chart shows a measure over time to spot trends, but has no control limits?
questions.explain: A run chart is a simple line over time.

questions.q: Which diagram maps the steps and decision points of a process, such as how a password reset request is handled?
questions.explain: Flowcharts show each step and branch in a process.

questions.q: Which chart shows completed work rising over time along with a separate line for total scope, so scope changes are visible?
questions.explain: A burnup chart shows both progress and any growth in scope.

questions.q: A sprint burndown line has stayed flat for three days. What does this suggest?
options: Little or no work is being completed, so the team may be blocked
The sprint is ahead of schedule
questions.explain: A flat burndown means remaining work is not dropping. Check for blockers.

questions.q: Which diagram shows the order of activities and their dependencies as boxes connected by arrows, used to find the critical path?
questions.explain: A network (precedence) diagram shows task logic.

questions.q: Which chart compares the story points a team completed in each of its recent sprints?
questions.explain: A velocity chart helps forecast how much work fits in future sprints.

questions.q: On a cumulative flow diagram, the 'In testing' band keeps getting wider. What does this mean?
options: Work is piling up in testing, which is a bottleneck
questions.explain: A widening band means items enter that stage faster than they leave.

questions.q: Which chart shows the reporting lines of people in the project or organisation?
questions.explain: The org chart shows who reports to whom.

questions.q: The team keeps asking 'why?' about a failed backup until it reaches the underlying cause. Which technique is this?
questions.explain: Asking why repeatedly moves past symptoms to the root cause.

questions.q: A technician makes a tally mark each time a certain defect type is found during inspection. Which tool is this?
questions.explain: Check sheets collect data quickly, often to feed a Pareto chart.

questions.q: Which tool plots risks on a grid by probability and impact, often coloured red, amber and green?
questions.explain: It shows which risks need attention first.

questions.q: Defects by cause: Configuration 50, Training 25, Hardware 15, Other 10. What percentage of defects come from the top two causes?
questions.explain: Total = 100. Configuration + Training = 75, which is 75%.

questions.q: Which tool maps out choices and their possible outcomes, with probabilities and values, to work out the best option?
questions.explain: Decision trees use expected monetary value to compare options.

questions.q: An option has a 60% chance of a $10,000 gain and a 40% chance of a $5,000 loss. What is its expected monetary value in dollars?
Executives want a simple view showing only the key dates, such as design sign-off and go-live. Which chart fits?
options: Detailed Gantt chart with every task
questions.explain: A milestone chart shows key points without task-level detail.

questions.q: Match each chart to the question it answers.
pairs: Which causes create most of the problems?
What could be causing this problem?
questions.explain: Pick the chart by the question you need answered.

learn.idea: An IT project manager does not need to configure servers, but must understand what the team is building, what it depends on and what can go wrong.
points: IaaS gives you servers and storage. PaaS gives you a platform to deploy code. SaaS gives you a finished application.
Cloud shifts spending from CapEx (buy up front) to OpEx (pay as you go).
RPO is how much data you can afford to lose. RTO is how long you can afford to be down.
Hot sites are ready to run at once. Warm sites need some setup. Cold sites are space and power only.
learn.memory: IaaS you manage the OS. PaaS you manage the code. SaaS you just use it.

cards.back: Rented servers, storage and networks. You manage the OS and up.
A platform to run your code. The provider manages the OS.
A complete application delivered over the internet, such as Microsoft 365.
Recovery point objective: the most data loss that is acceptable.
Recovery time objective: the most downtime that is acceptable.
Hot is ready to take over at once. Cold has space and power but no equipment ready.

questions.q: A company rents virtual servers, storage and networking from a cloud provider, and its own team manages the operating systems. Which service model is this?
questions.explain: With IaaS the provider runs the hardware and you manage everything from the OS up.

questions.q: Developers upload their code to a cloud platform that handles the servers, operating system and runtime for them. Which model is this?
questions.explain: PaaS lets developers focus on code while the provider runs the platform.

questions.q: Staff use a web-based email and office suite that the vendor fully runs and updates. Which model is this?
questions.explain: SaaS delivers a complete application. You just use it.

questions.q: An organisation keeps sensitive systems in its own data centre but bursts extra workloads to a public cloud. What is this?
questions.explain: Hybrid cloud combines private or on-premises resources with public cloud.

questions.q: How does moving from on-premises servers to the cloud usually change project spending?
options: From capital expenses (CapEx) to operating expenses (OpEx)
From operating expenses to capital expenses
It has no effect on costs
questions.explain: Cloud is usually paid monthly as used, instead of buying hardware up front.

questions.q: Which technology lets one physical server run many separate virtual machines?
questions.explain: Hypervisors such as VMware ESXi or KVM share one host's hardware among many VMs.

questions.q: Which device spreads incoming web traffic across several servers so no single one is overloaded?
questions.explain: Load balancers improve performance and availability.

questions.q: Which component stores and organises application data such as customer records so it can be queried?
questions.explain: Applications usually keep their data in a database server.

questions.q: Remote staff need secure access to internal systems over the internet. Which technology is commonly used?
questions.explain: A VPN creates an encrypted tunnel over the internet.

questions.q: Users at a branch office say the new app is slow because each request takes a long time to reach the data centre. Which term describes this delay?
questions.explain: Latency is delay. Bandwidth is how much data can move at once.

questions.q: The project design adds a second power supply and a second network link to a critical server so one failure does not stop it. What is this?
questions.explain: Redundancy removes single points of failure.

questions.q: The business says it can lose no more than one hour of data if the system fails. Which value is this?
questions.explain: RPO is about data loss and drives how often backups run.

questions.q: A disaster recovery site has equipment, current data and network links ready to take over almost at once. What type of site is this?
questions.explain: Hot sites cost the most but recover fastest.

questions.q: In the cloud shared responsibility model for IaaS, who is usually responsible for patching the guest operating system?
questions.explain: With IaaS the provider secures the physical layer and hypervisor. The customer manages the OS.

questions.q: An online shop's cloud servers add capacity during a holiday sale and remove it after. What is this called?
questions.explain: Elasticity scales resources up and down with demand.

questions.q: New storage arrays for the project have a ten-week delivery time. What should the PM do?
options: Order them early and treat the lead time as a schedule dependency and risk
Wait until the build phase to order
Ignore it, vendors always deliver early
questions.explain: Long hardware lead times are a common cause of IT project delays.

learn.idea: Code moves from development through testing to production. In live IT systems, changes are controlled so a project cannot break what the business depends on.
