points: Environments: development, test (QA), staging, production.
UAT is done by real users to confirm the solution meets their needs.
Every production change needs a rollback (backout) plan and usually a maintenance window.
ITIL change types: standard (pre-approved), normal (CAB review), emergency (urgent fix).
learn.memory: Dev, Test, Stage, Prod. Never test in prod.

cards.back: Development, test, staging, production.
User acceptance testing: end users confirm it meets their needs.
Re-testing to make sure old features still work after a change.
Steps to undo a change and restore the previous state.
Low-risk, pre-approved, done often, such as a routine password reset.
Release to a small group first, then everyone.

questions.q: Put the environments in the order code normally moves through them.
questions.explain: Each step is closer to the real system, so problems are caught before users see them.

questions.q: Before go-live, accounts staff test the new finance system with real tasks to confirm it meets their needs. Which testing is this?
questions.explain: UAT is done by the business users, not the developers.

questions.q: After a bug fix, the team re-runs earlier tests to make sure existing features still work. Which testing is this?
questions.explain: Regression testing catches new changes breaking old features.

questions.q: Match each test type to what it checks.
pairs: One small piece of code on its own
Basic functions work after a deployment
questions.explain: Testing builds up from small pieces to the whole system.

questions.q: The server upgrade will take the email system offline. When should it be scheduled?
options: During an approved maintenance window with users notified
In the middle of the business day without notice
questions.explain: Maintenance windows are agreed low-impact times for planned changes.

questions.q: What must be prepared before a production change, in case it goes wrong?
questions.explain: A rollback plan restores the previous working state if the change fails.

questions.q: Match each ITIL change type to its description.
pairs: Assessed and approved by the CAB
Urgent fix with a fast-track approval
questions.explain: The change type decides how much review is needed.

questions.q: In IT operations, which group reviews and approves normal changes to production systems?
questions.explain: The CAB checks risk, timing and impact before production changes.

questions.q: A new desktop image is deployed to one department first, then to the whole company once it works well. What is this approach?
questions.explain: A pilot limits the impact of any problems.

questions.q: The old and new payroll systems run side by side for one month so results can be compared before the old one is switched off. What is this?
questions.explain: Parallel running is safest but costs more effort.

questions.q: Code changes are automatically built, tested and prepared for release each time a developer commits. What is this practice?
questions.explain: CI/CD catches problems early and makes releases routine.

questions.q: Two weeks before go-live, the team stops adding new features and only fixes bugs. What is this called?
questions.explain: A code freeze keeps the release stable for final testing.

questions.q: If a project engineer is sure a production change is safe, it can skip the operational change control process.
questions.explain: Production changes follow the organisation's change process, however safe they seem. Unapproved changes are a common cause of outages.

questions.q: Right after deployment, the team quickly checks that users can log in and the main pages load. What is this?
questions.explain: Smoke tests are fast checks that the release basically works.

learn.idea: IT projects must follow laws, regulations and company policies. Knowing which rules apply to the data you handle shapes the design, the vendors and the schedule.
points: PII is any data that can identify a person.
GDPR protects personal data of people in the EU. HIPAA protects US health data. PCI DSS protects card data. SOX covers US public company financial controls.
Data retention policies say how long records are kept and when they are destroyed.
Some laws require data to stay in certain countries (data sovereignty).
learn.memory: GDPR people, HIPAA patients, PCI cards, SOX books.

cards.back: Personally identifiable information: data that can identify someone.
Personal data of people in the EU.
US protected health information.
Payment card data.
Financial reporting controls at US public companies.
Data is subject to the laws of the country where it is stored.

questions.q: Which is personally identifiable information (PII)?
options: A customer's full name with their national ID number
The number of servers in a rack
The average CPU use of a cluster
The colour of a company logo
questions.explain: PII can identify a specific person, alone or combined with other data.

questions.q: A Jamaican company's new web app collects personal data from customers living in France. Which regulation is most likely to apply?
questions.explain: GDPR protects people in the EU, wherever the company is based.

questions.q: A project builds a patient records system for a US hospital. Which regulation applies to the health data?
questions.explain: HIPAA protects US health information.

questions.q: An online store will accept credit card payments. Which standard applies to the card data?
questions.explain: PCI DSS sets security rules for anyone that stores, processes or sends card data.

questions.q: A US public company is changing its financial reporting system. Which law requires strong controls and audit trails over financial reporting?
questions.explain: SOX requires accurate financial reporting and controls.

questions.q: Which policy says how long the organisation must keep records and when they must be destroyed?
questions.explain: Retention policies balance legal needs, cost and privacy.

questions.q: Which data classification usually needs the strongest protection?
questions.explain: Classification levels decide how data must be handled and protected.

questions.q: A government agency requires its citizen data to stay on servers inside its own country. What concept is this?
questions.explain: Data is subject to the laws of where it is stored, so location can be mandated.

questions.q: The design team collects only the customer fields the new app really needs. Which privacy principle is this?
questions.explain: Collecting less data reduces privacy risk and compliance work.

questions.q: Which group provides oversight, approves major decisions and resolves escalations across a large project?
questions.explain: Governance bodies keep projects aligned with the organisation's goals.

questions.q: Auditors need to see who changed which records and when. What must the system keep?
questions.explain: Audit trails provide accountability and are required by many regulations.

questions.q: A public sector website must be usable by people with disabilities, such as those using screen readers. What should the project follow?
questions.explain: Accessibility is often a legal and policy requirement for public services.

questions.q: The team wants to install a tool on 200 PCs. What should be checked first?
options: That the organisation has enough valid licences
That it has a nice logo
That the vendor has an MOU
Nothing, software is free to copy
questions.explain: Using software beyond its licence terms is a legal and financial risk.

questions.q: Under GDPR, a customer asks the company to delete their personal data. Which right is this?
options: Right to erasure (right to be forgotten)
questions.explain: GDPR gives people the right to have their data erased in many cases.

questions.q: A new data protection regulation takes effect halfway through the project and affects the design. What should the PM do?
options: Assess the impact and raise a change request
Ignore it until the next project
Tell the team to keep going as planned
questions.explain: Compliance changes go through change control like any other change.

questions.q: Compliance requirements should be identified early in the project, since they can affect design, vendors, cost and schedule.
questions.explain: Finding a compliance need late often means expensive rework.

learn.idea: Security is part of the project from day one, not a check at the end. Protect access, protect data, and plan for incidents.
points: Least privilege: give people only the access they need.
MFA adds a second factor beyond the password.
Encrypt data at rest (stored) and in transit (moving).
CIA triad: confidentiality, integrity, availability.
learn.memory: C-I-A: keep it secret, keep it correct, keep it running.

cards.back: Only the minimum access needed to do the job.
Two or more factors: something you know, have or are.

cards.front: Encryption at rest vs in transit?
cards.back: At rest protects stored data. In transit protects data moving over a network.
Confidentiality, integrity, availability.
Split critical tasks so no one person can misuse them alone.
Securely wipe or destroy them and keep a record.

questions.q: A contractor needs to update one web application. What access should they get?
options: Only the access needed for that application, for the time needed
The same access as the CIO
questions.explain: Least privilege limits the damage if an account is misused.

questions.q: Users must enter a password and then approve a prompt on their phone to log in. What is this?
questions.explain: MFA combines something you know with something you have or are.

questions.q: The new system stores customer files on disk and sends them over the internet. How should they be protected?
options: Encrypt them at rest and in transit
questions.explain: Encryption protects data whether it is stored or moving.

questions.q: Which is a physical security control for a new server room?
questions.explain: Physical controls stop people reaching the hardware.

questions.q: Staff keep clicking fake emails that ask for their passwords. What helps most?
questions.explain: Phishing is social engineering, and training is a key defence.

questions.q: Before the new web portal goes live, what security step should be planned?
options: A vulnerability scan or security test, with findings fixed
Nothing, security is checked after launch
Sharing the admin password with the team
questions.explain: Security testing before go-live finds problems while they are cheap to fix.

questions.q: One person can both create a new supplier and approve payments to it. What control is missing?
questions.explain: Splitting critical tasks stops one person committing and hiding fraud.

questions.q: Testers want a copy of production customer data in the test environment. What should be done?
options: Mask or anonymise the personal data first
Post it on the shared drive
questions.explain: Test environments are less protected, so real personal data should be masked.

questions.q: At the end of a hardware refresh project, what should happen to the old hard drives?
options: Securely wipe or destroy them and keep a record
Put them in the normal bin
questions.explain: Drives can hold sensitive data. Sanitise or destroy them and keep proof.

questions.q: During the project, the team finds signs that a test server was broken into. What should they do first?
options: Follow the incident response plan and report it right away
Keep working and mention it at the next status meeting
questions.explain: Incident response contains the damage and preserves evidence.

questions.q: A contractor finishes their work on the project. What should happen to their access?
options: Remove it promptly as part of offboarding
Leave it in case they come back
questions.explain: Old accounts are a common way in for attackers.

questions.q: Match each part of the CIA triad to its meaning.
pairs: Only authorised people can see the data
Data is accurate and not changed without permission
Systems and data are there when needed
questions.explain: Every security control supports one or more of these three goals.
